title: Rethinking Easy-to-Hard: Limits of Curriculum Learning in Post-Training for Deductive Reasoning
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether curriculum learning—especially easy-to-hard ordering of training examples—improves large language model post-training for deductive reasoning. The authors note that curriculum learning is widely used and intuitively appealing for compositional reasoning tasks, where harder problems are built from simpler inference steps, but that its actual value in LLM post-training has not been systematically established.

To study this question, the paper compares several curriculum schedules against standard random sampling during post-training. The experiments use synthetic arithmetic and logical reasoning datasets with explicitly defined structural difficulty, allowing the authors to test whether ordering examples by difficulty affects out-of-distribution generalization to harder problems. They evaluate both supervised fine-tuning on reasoning traces and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards across multiple medium-sized open-weight language models.

The study does not involve human learners, teachers, or K-12 educational settings. Instead, the "population" is a set of language models trained and evaluated on synthetic benchmarks including MathGAP arithmetic tasks and knights-and-knaves logic problems. The work is conducted in a computational/online experimental setting rather than a classroom or school context.

The main conclusion is that curriculum learning provides no robust or consistent advantage over standard random sampling for deductive reasoning post-training under a fixed training budget. Across datasets, model families, and training methods, the ordering of examples had little effect on accuracy or response length. The authors further report that reinforcement learning generally improved out-of-distribution performance more reliably than supervised fine-tuning, while supervised fine-tuning could sometimes underperform even zero-shot baselines. Overall, the paper argues that example sequencing is less important than feedback mechanisms and training data structure for compositional reasoning.
quality_tier_rationale: This paper is an AI/ML methods study on curriculum learning for post-training large language models on synthetic deductive reasoning benchmarks, not a K-12 education intervention study. It provides no school-based sample, no learner population, and no direct educational evaluation relevant to K-12 literacy evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports no direct K-12 educational outcomes and therefore cannot contribute evidence on literacy or related student impacts. Its main empirical conclusion is also null within its own technical context: curriculum-based sequencing showed no robust advantage over standard sampling.
